When do educational expectations motivate effort? Expectation-opportunity alignment and study time across 27 countries
abstract: Educational expectations are widely assumed to motivate student effort, yet their effectiveness may depend on broader opportunity structures. Using data from the 2018 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) across 27 countries and economies, this study investigates (a) the association between expectations for higher education and study time, and (b) how this relationship varies cross-nationally. Country-specific regressions show that, while expectations predict greater study time in many contexts, associations are insignificant elsewhere. Multilevel models further reveal that, on average, higher educational expectations correspond to significantly more study time; however, the strength of this association systematically depends on the alignment between a country's prevalence of educational expectations and its rate of higher education enrollment. The results demonstrate an inverted U-shaped pattern, where expectations strongly predict effort when aspirations and opportunities are well-aligned, but lose their significance under conditions of either scarcity or abundance of opportunity. These findings highlight the conditional nature of students' motivational responses to expectations and the importance of contextual opportunity structures in shaping academic effort.

title: Editorial Board
Answering the call: How changes to the salience of job characteristics affect college students’ decisions
abstract: College students often make employment decisions with incomplete information, particularly about compensation. As a result, they may rely on misleading heuristics (such as assuming that interesting or prosocial jobs pay badly) and overlook campus positions that would support both their financial needs and their development. We test whether highlighting job characteristics changes students' application behavior in a preregistered field experiment and find that it does. Increasing the salience of a tutoring job's monetary benefits nearly tripled application rates (a 196% increase). In contrast, messages emphasizing prosocial, career, or social benefits had no effect, despite students reporting these as their primary motivations for applying. The study highlights the incongruencies in college students' decision making alongside a simple, low-cost strategy for recruiting college students to enriching campus jobs.

title: Job loss and births. A couple-level study of Norwegian plant closures
abstract: In dual-earner settings, whether fertility responses to job loss reflect gendered mechanisms is not theoretically unambiguous. This paper examines how job loss due to plant closures – a plausibly exogenous employment shock – affects couples' fertility in Norway. Using Norwegian register data (2005-2017) linked to private-sector employment records (2005-2014), we estimate discrete-time event history models of first- and second-birth transitions within three years after a plant-closure job loss experienced by either partner. Norway is a theoretically relevant case because welfare-state buffering limits short-run income losses, and the Great Recession hit relatively mildly, helping explore the role of uncertainty in shaping fertility responses to job loss. Results indicate that job loss disrupts childbirth in gendered and stratified ways. Female partner's job loss in a couple reduces entry into parenthood, and this effect persists net of household income at the time of job loss. Male partner job loss in a couple reduces progression to a second child and is partly mediated by income, and is strongest after the Great Recession. Moreover, couples with fewer resources are more exposed to fertility penalties, especially for second births following male displacement. The limited role of income suggests that fertility responses to job loss are not reducible to short-run financial constraints. Instead, they reflect how employment structures couples' life-course planning and perceived readiness for parenthood. That female job loss deters entry into parenthood while male job loss deters expansion implies that economic-role convergence has not paralleled convergence in the social meaning of job loss. • Female partner's job loss reduces the likelihood of entering parenthood. • Male partner's job loss reduces the probability of family expansion. • This negative effect persists net of household income at the time of job loss. • Couples with lower income before male job loss face greater second birth penalties.

title: Socioeconomic divides in curricular pathways: Unpacking decision-making mechanisms and peer effects
abstract: This study develops and tests a comprehensive framework to explain socioeconomic inequalities in curricular choices, using England as a test case. Drawing on rational choice theory, bounded rationality, behavioural science, and culturalist perspectives, we evaluate a broad set of explanatory mechanisms. Linking rich survey data to administrative records, we examine both individual-level factors and peer effects, employing for the latter an instrumental variable approach based on the peer-of-peer methodology. We find that a parsimonious model incorporating prior academic performance, a composite measure of subjective occupational returns capturing the perceived accessibility of higher education and decision uncertainty, and peer influences fully accounts for observed socioeconomic disparities in curricular choices. Leveraging longitudinal data, we demonstrate that the balance between expressive and instrumental motivations for curricular choices shifts over time, with growing importance accorded to the latter at later educational transitions.

title: Employment stability and social origin: Cumulative advantages in young adults’ homeownership and financial asset accumulation
abstract: Millennials experience marked intra-cohort inequalities in asset ownership. In line with the cumulative advantage theory, we posit that school-to-work (STW) transitions and social origins are joint drivers of these disparities. Using prospective longitudinal data from the UK, we employ sequence and cluster analysis to develop a typology of STW trajectories (age 16-25). We then estimate the relationship between this typology and homeownership and financial assets at age 32, while also assessing its predictive value when controlling for income. Finally, we examine the heterogeneities of the STW-asset nexus by social origin. Our findings indicate that: (i) young adults with high-churn or intermittent economic activities, as well as those in prolonged periods of unemployment or inactivity, are less likely to have ever owned a home or hold any financial assets; (ii) advantaged social origins, proxied by parental service class occupation and parental homeownership in adolescence, cumulatively propel the asset outcomes of young adults with already “successful” STW transitions, in part through direct financial support for their first home purchase. This suggests that sustained employment generates a stability premium toward asset accumulation that is both driven and amplified by social origin.

title: A Schumpeter hotel? Surname status inequality and persistence in Sweden, 1880–2015
abstract: Conventional social mobility research misses substantial inequalities of opportunity. To capture intergenerational persistence of family social status, we need to move beyond parent-child associations in occupation or income. We study the inheritance of surname status as a group-level process, using full-count population data for Sweden between 1880 and 2015 and surname types reflecting pre-industrial social strata. Our analyses show that social stratification by surnames occurs primarily at the level of surname types associated with pre-industrial social strata, rather than at the level of individual lineages, especially before 1950. Surname status inequality is remarkably high in 1880 but declines substantially by 2015. Surname status persistence, on the other hand, is nearly as high in the modern Swedish welfare state as in preindustrial times. Surname groups converge in status at a slow rate, with differences persisting over at least six generations. Structural transformation and the emergence of the welfare state have only implied a limited decline in surname status persistence. As a group, families with an agricultural or working-class surname backgrounds (patronyms) experience a persistent disadvantage, while noble and educated surnames display a persistent advantage. Hence, surname status persistence is not only an elite phenomenon but shapes patterns of intergenerational persistence across social classes.

title: Variation and change in high school STEM opportunity to learn in the US: Is the organization of the STEM curriculum functional or conflict driven?
The role of gender in gene by family SES interactions – A twin study across four European countries
abstract: Studies of gene-by-family socioeconomic status (GxSES) interactions in educational outcomes have yielded mixed findings. Building on a socio-contextual perspective, this study emphasizes that genetic influences are shaped not only by family environments but also by broader social forces, including gender and institutional context. Prior sociogenetic research, for example, suggests that early school tracking may suppress genetic influences. Using large twin registers from Finland, Norway, Germany, and the Netherlands, we analyzed gene-by-environment interactions by parental education and child gender, employing non-parametric gene–environment interaction models. Our results showed that genetic influences in Germany were weaker, and shared environmental effects were stronger, than in the other countries. We found no significant gender differences in the magnitude of genetic or environmental effects on educational attainment. Analyses of GxSES revealed that the form and strength of interactions depend on both gender and country context. In most countries, we observed a negative interaction among women, meaning that genetic influences were weaker among individuals from high-SES families. Among men, GxSES varied across contexts, appearing positive, negative, or absent. We conclude that country context and gender shape gene-by-SES interactions in educational attainment and may help explain the mixed results reported in previous GxSES studies.

title: From margins to mainstream: Migrant experiences and intergenerational transmission of educational aspiration in urban China
Corrigendum to “Educational assortative mating and changing patterns of parental financial investment in children, 1990–2024” [Soc. Sci. Res. 136C (2026) 103347]
Secularization and low fertility: How declining church membership changes couples’ childbearing
abstract: Previous studies have shown that secularization altered historical Western fertility patterns, but few studies have addressed the role of religion in the marked fertility declines in recent decades. We examine the relationship between secularization and fertility decline in Finland from a couple perspective, amid a broader trend of declining fertility. We show that secularization can exert a self-reinforcing negative effect on fertility through an interplay of declining church membership and childbearing of religiously mixed and homogeneous couples. Using data from the Finnish administrative registers covering the period from 1995 to 2019, we are able to identify religious affiliation, as measured by church tax payments in the secularized context of Finland. The analysis takes a dyadic perspective to explore the relationships between couples’ religious affiliation and their probability of having a first child. We conclude that the accelerated decline in church membership has contributed to the recent fertility decline.

title: No quick fix: Experimental evidence on whether school safety information mitigates anti-black perceptions and preferences for schools
abstract: Race-based discrimination and segregation are persistent realities in the United States. Theories of biased stereotypes and statistical discrimination suggest that increasing information could counter racialized beliefs, choices, and resulting inequalities. This study examines whether increased school safety information alters anti-Black school evaluations through a survey experiment with 1,125 non-Black parents. Participants evaluated school profiles with randomized racial demographics, with some respondents receiving school safety information. Results demonstrate that non-Black parents perceived Black schools as less supportive, more violent, and academically weaker than otherwise similar White, Asian, and Latine schools. They also preferred to enroll their students in White, Asian, Latine schools over Black schools. Importantly, providing additional information about school safety, on average, did not alter parents' anti-Black beliefs about schools nor their desires to avoid Black schools. However, this aggregate null effect obscures important heterogeneity: safety information partially attenuated racialized beliefs for some demographic groups but amplified anti-Black beliefs among others. Results suggest that providing information may not be enough to fully curtail the racial biases and stereotypes that underlie racialized evaluations and segregation.

title: Professional patterns: Occupation-Specific health behavior profiles
On your mark, get set, go: A multilevel analysis of racial residential segregation in U.S. metropolitan areas
abstract: Residential segregation research has largely proceeded along two separate tracks: aggregate-level analyses that predict segregation scores with metropolitan characteristics, and household-level studies that model locational attainments using individual attributes. This study bridges these traditions by applying a multilevel meta-regression framework to examine how metropolitan-level contexts shape White–Black, White–Latino, and White–Asian residential segregation patterns across 25 U.S. metropolitan areas. Using previously estimated coefficients from household-level locational attainment models reported in Crowell and Fossett (2022) as dependent variables in a two-step meta regression with random effects, and metropolitan-level characteristics from the 2008–2012 American Community Survey and 2010 Decennial Census as level-2 predictors, we assess how contextual factors both directly influence segregation and moderate returns on household resources such as income, education, and nativity. Our findings reveal that the locus of White locational attainment advantage varies across group comparisons. For White–Black segregation, advantage is overwhelmingly concentrated in the regression constants, indicating that group membership itself—rather than differential returns on socioeconomic resources—drives segregation, consistent with place stratification theory. For White–Latino and White–Asian comparisons, the balance between structural group membership effects and resource returns shifts more variably across metropolitan contexts. Metropolitan characteristics also matter: regional location predicts White–Black segregation, while minoritized population growth predicts White–Latino and White–Asian segregation, consistent with group threat theory. Furthermore, we find an inverse relationship between gaps in the constants and gaps in returns on resources, suggesting that the extent to which spatial assimilation can operate depends on how deeply entrenched structural inequality already is. These findings demonstrate the value of linking micro- and macro-level dimensions of segregation to illuminate the complexity of racial stratification processes.

title: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and perceived intergenerational mobility in Czechia and Uruguay. An unexpected event during survey design study
abstract: Can large-scale geopolitical shocks causally reshape how individuals perceive their intergenerational mobility? War unsettles everyday life through security fears, policy uncertainty, inflation, and energy shocks—factors that can recalibrate the benchmarks people use when comparing their lives to their parents’. We address this question by examining the immediate impact of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on mobility perceptions using a quasi-experimental design. Leveraging World Values Survey fieldwork occurring in Czechia and Uruguay around Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, we compare respondents interviewed immediately before and after February 24, 2022 within an unexpected event during survey design. Using the quasi-random interview dates around the invasion, we find consistent null effects across multiple specifications—including bandwidth sensitivity analyses, logit models, robust bias-corrected estimates, demographic controls, and placebo tests. The invasion produced no discernible immediate impact on either upward or downward mobility perceptions in either country, despite Czechia’s geographic proximity and historical ties to the region. These findings complement prior correlational evidence showing associations between war concerns and mobility beliefs one year after the invasion, suggesting that such effects may unfold gradually rather than instantaneously, or that correlational patterns reflect selection into worry rather than immediate causal impacts. By establishing a causal upper bound on the immediate effect of invasion exposure on mobility perceptions, our findings constrain the plausible magnitude of causal effects in a literature built primarily on observational evidence.

title: The good, the bad, and the healthy: A factorial survey analysis of situational morality in consumption and healthcare
Editorial Board
Motherhood and access to top positions: The one percent glass-ceiling under Nordic family policies
Gender convergence of cannabis use, dependence, and risk in the U.S.
abstract: Historically, males exhibited higher prevalence of cannabis use, greater dependence, and viewed cannabis as less risky. However, as U.S. cannabis policy shifts rapidly, accompanied by cultural changes in normalization and destigmatization, research has been mixed on whether the male-female gap is increasing or decreasing. Using twenty years (2002-2021) of nationally representative National Survey on Drug Use and Health data and Age-Period-Cohort-Interaction (APC-I) models, we examined trends by gender in past-month and daily cannabis use, dependence, and risk perceptions. Framed within the Theory of Constrained Choices and by highlighting the interdependency of age-period-cohort over time, we demonstrate substantial overall gender convergence across all four cannabis metrics. While this convergence over time was especially pronounced in adolescence and early adulthood, some degree of convergence has occurred for at least some outcomes across all age groups. The form of convergence varied by outcome and life course stage within the same outcome. Generally, convergence seen in any past month use and dependence among adolescents is driven by decreases among males and stable or rising female values, while convergence in daily use is from rising female consumption. Convergence in use and dependence at age 21 and older is typically driven by greater increases among females. Perceptions of risk decreased considerably for both, but especially for females, narrowing gaps across age groups. Sub-analyses indicate that convergence occurred similarly across policy contexts. This convergence underscores that prevention and intervention efforts should continue to incorporate gender-specific needs to improve population health due to differing impacts of comparable use.

title: Horizontal stratification and educational homogamy in South Korea: Marriage patterns and preferences across elite- and non-elite university graduates
Americans' views of religion in public life: The effect of three cultural models on attitudes toward religious and nonreligious groups
abstract: This paper investigates the relation between Americans’ cultural models of religion in public life, and views of religious groups in American society. We explicate how three dominant cultural models, Christian nationalism, civil religion, and liberal secularism, influence attitudes toward atheists, Buddhists, Muslims, Jews, LDS (Mormons), and Conservative Christians. Do survey respondents see each religious group as consistent with their vision of the ideal American society? Using the national survey data available in the American Mosaic Study of 2014, we find that Christian nationalism and civil religion operate in distinct ways to shape views of religious and nonreligious outgroups. We find evidence that Christian nationalists oppose Muslims, atheists, and other religious groups in public life, with the exception of conservative Christians, Jews and LDS. Civil religionists are more open to a pluralistic public square and thus have more positive views of most other religions. Liberal secularists favor atheists but are generally opposed to religious groups in their vision of American society, especially conservative Christians and Mormons.

title: Depressive symptom trajectories from adolescence to midlife among Latin Americans in the United States: Variation by generation and region of origin
abstract: Prior research on health disparities among Latin Americans in the United States has often yielded inconclusive findings, likely due to diverse immigrant generations and national origins. To examine how depressive symptoms evolve from adolescence through midlife among U.S. Latin Americans, we analyzed five waves of data from 3,525 self-identified Hispanic/Latino participants in the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health. Depressive symptoms were measured at five time points using a psychometrically validated four-item CES-D scale, with missing data handled via multiple imputation. We estimated depressive symptom trajectories using mixed-effects Poisson models specifying a quartic polynomial age specification, modeling longitudinal disparities across immigrant generations and regions of origin. This approach allowed us to examine generation and region of origin main effects and their age interactions. Results show that first-generation immigrants consistently exhibit lower depressive symptoms than their third-plus-generation counterparts, with second-generation immigrants in between. Social support and region of origin largely account for these generational differences, with social support largely explaining the second-generation advantage and substantially attenuating the first-generation advantage. Analyses by national origin also reveal a persistent Puerto Rican disadvantage and a stable Cuban American advantage, relative to the Mexican American referent, which are robust to adjusting for race, generation, or socioeconomic status. Linear mixed-effects models were used as a robustness check, confirming these findings. Overall, results underscore how structural and cultural factors shape mental health outcomes within the U.S. Latin American population, highlighting the importance of disaggregated analyses and life course-sensitive frameworks for understanding depressive symptom disparities.

title: Socialite or sociable? Highbrow tastes, omnivorous inclinations, and perceptions of individuals’ status and qualities
abstract: Sociologists argue that cultural tastes shape perceptions of individuals’ status and personal qualities. Yet it remains unclear whether highbrow and omnivorous tastes create different perceptions. To address this gap, we designed two vignette survey experiments to identify the effect of highbrow (vs. lowbrow) and omnivorous (vs. univorous) tastes on a wide range of perceptions. Results for Denmark, replicated in two experiments, show that while highbrow (vs. lowbrow) tastes elicit favorable perceptions of status, labor market success, and sophistication (i.e., being high-class, high-earning, and cultured), omnivorous (vs. univorous) tastes mainly elicit favorable perceptions of sociability (i.e., being socially oriented and warm). Supplementary analyses of qualitative text data corroborate these findings, including that omnivorous tastes elicit favorable perceptions of sociability. Finally, highbrow and omnivorous tastes create clearer perceptions of status, measured by lower variance in ratings of status. We end by addressing the implications of our results for research on cultural taste, labor markets, elites, and intersectional inequality.

title: The intergenerational mobility advantage of educators’ children: Capital embedded in occupations
Catalysts and buffers: How diversity and status in social networks shape attitudes towards inequality in contemporary societies
abstract: This paper explores how the socioeconomic composition of individuals' social networks shapes attitudes towards inequality in contemporary societies. While limited cross-national research has examined the location of people's acquaintances within the social structure, this study fills a crucial gap by jointly analyzing their heterogeneity and concentration. Using data from the ISSP 2017 Social Networks Module, the study investigates how socioeconomic network diversity and status relate to perceptions of inequality and preferences for redistribution across 32,310 individuals in 31 countries. Country fixed-effects regression results indicate that individuals with more socioeconomically diverse networks show modestly higher national inequality perceptions, whereas having higher-status acquaintances is strongly associated with lower support for redistribution. These effects are not uniform: network diversity often acts as a catalyst and network status as a buffer of distributive attitudes. Social networks thus operate simultaneously as comparative frames (highlighting disparities) and reference frames (anchoring norms), amplifying or dampening individuals' views on inequality. Notably, network effects operate consistently across all socioeconomic groups, regardless of individuals' SES. Overall, the study advances meso-level perspectives on distributive justice by demonstrating how everyday social relationships shape perceptions and beliefs about inequality in stratified societies.

title: Toward a formal sociological model of partner search
Corrigendum to ‘Do sanctuary policies increase crime? Contrary evidence from a county-level investigation in the United States’ [Soc. Sci. Res. 106 (2022) 102743]
The role of sanitary pads in school achievement in low-income settings
abstract: Educational attainment and achievement are key areas of study for social scientists because they are associated with a wide range of outcomes, including income, careers, marriage, fertility, migration, and longevity. Using unique multimethod, longitudinal data from Nepal, a low-income setting, we explore how the availability of sanitary pads in restrooms is associated with school achievement. We focus on eighth grade students, marking a pivotal time in which many female students begin menstruating. Multilevel modeling estimates reveal that the availability of sanitary pads in school restrooms have a statistically significant positive association with an increase in language test scores for females. The results also show a positive association between the availability of sanitary pads and an increase in math and science test scores, but these associations are not statistically significant. These findings reveal that school hygiene facilities can play an important role in school achievement, which can shape students' matriculation into the next academic year and potential longer-term consequences including both academic and social outcomes, such as school dropout, income, and marriage timing.

title: Risk, return, and resonance: Symbolic considerations in everyday stock selection
abstract: How do retail investors choose which stocks to own? While finance models assume investors maximize risk-adjusted returns, and economic sociology has long argued that markets are culturally embedded, we lack systematic quantitative evidence on how symbolic considerations--values alignment, identity expression, and social ties--shape ordinary stock selection. Drawing on two original studies of U.S. retail investors, we estimate the relative importance of symbolic versus financial attributes in stated stock choice and examine how investors narrate attachment to stocks they actually own. Study 1, a choice-based conjoint experiment, shows that investors allocate roughly forty percent of their decision weight to non-financial attributes when these attributes are made salient, with values/identity alignment emerging as the third most important factor after expected return and risk. Study 2, a survey of stockholders, finds that investors report similar levels of identity attachment to a favored stock as to a favored consumer brand, which suggests that shares, just like consumer goods, are subject to symbolic consumption. Cluster analysis identifies three segments of investor self-understanding: financial-focused (37%), values/meaning-driven (47%), and socially-connected (16%). These findings show that symbolic considerations are not confined to spectacular cases such as meme stocks or ESG investing; they appear as measurable components of ordinary investments.

title: Reassessing the gendered link between maternal employment and adult children's labor market participation: A trajectory-based approach
abstract: Although maternal employment has long been linked to children's later labor market outcomes, most research treats employment as a static status rather than an evolving process across childhood. This study reassesses the relationship between maternal employment and adult children's labor market participation by adopting a trajectory-based perspective that captures the dynamic nature of mothers' work patterns, with particular attention paid to timing and intensity. Drawing on mother-child dyadic longitudinal data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (1979) (NLSY79) and the NLSY79 Child and Young Adult (n = 2,186), this study applies sequence analysis to classify distinct patterns of maternal employment trajectories across children's childhood and random-effects multinomial logit models with inverse probability of treatment weighting to assess how these trajectories predict adult children's labor market participation. Five trajectories emerge: continuously full-time, early return, late return, part-time, and not working. Relative to continuously full-time employment, a not-working trajectory is associated with a substantially higher likelihood of non-employment in adulthood for both sons and daughters, though the association for sons weakens after accounting for pre-birth family background. Part-time and late-return trajectories predict higher odds of reduced employment only among daughters. These findings underscore the gendered nature of intergenerational transmission in labor market participation.

title: Do people stay ‘hunkered down’ in diverse spaces? A longitudinal analysis of positive and negative social contact and the development of trust in linguistically diverse areas
abstract: The constrict thesis hypothesises that people ‘hunker down’ or withdraw from social and civic life in the face of migrant and ethnic diversity, degrading the collective social capital and cohesion of diverse communities. The large body of research since has focused on the second part of this thesis: the relationship between diversity and social capital and cohesion and the moderating role of the wider urban ecology, neglecting the first part: whether people are engaged and socially connected within diverse spaces or whether they withdraw and hunker down. In this study, we draw on longitudinal survey data from Australia to quantitatively examine both aspects, analysing and projecting trajectories of pro- and anti-social behaviours and trust in linguistically diverse areas. The results suggest that pro-social behaviours become more common the longer people have lived in diverse areas, while hostility between neighbours declines. This finding is argued to be important for understanding processes of intergroup contact and the development of intercultural harmony. Indeed, the results suggest that while an element of hunkering down in diverse spaces appears at play, this can with time and enabling conditions give way to greater sociability and cohesion in diverse spaces.

title: Degrees of engagement: Higher education, gender, and civic participation in South Korea
‘Reading between the lies’: Reading achievement, socioeconomic inequality, and adolescents' resistance to misinformation
abstract: In this hyperconnected world, misinformation spreads faster and farther than ever before. Adolescents, navigating the challenges of growing up, may be especially vulnerable to the overwhelming flow of digital information, including content on globally shared social media platforms. This study examines adolescents’ resistance to misinformation across 49 countries, using novel measures from the 2022 Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) dataset. We construct a composite index of misinformation resistance, capturing aspects such as checking accuracy, comparing sources, and sharing unverified content. Descriptive patterns show that most students compare sources and check accuracy, but many still trust or share unverified information, with notable socioeconomic status (SES) and regional disparities. Multilevel regression models show a positive, significant association between reading achievement and misinformation resistance. Importantly, the SES gap in misinformation resistance is largest among students at the bottom of the reading achievement distribution, but is not significant among those at the top of the achievement distribution. We argue that closing digital literacy gaps between advantaged and disadvantaged students requires investments in both literacy skills and awareness of misinformation.

title: Impact of subsidized childcare on maternal employment: A comparative study on native and migrant women in Germany
abstract: This study explores the impact of subsidized childcare on maternal employment, focusing on the heterogeneous effects of Germany's Childcare Funding Act (2013) on native and first- and second-generation migrant mothers. Despite lower childcare use and higher unemployment rates among migrant women, research on this topic has been limited. Using the SOEP dataset from 2010 to 2019 and a triple difference approach, we find that subsidized childcare significantly increases maternal employment, particularly for mothers with children aged 2, with lasting effects. However, migrant women's policy responses remain lower than that of natives and no significant differences are observed between the first- and second-generation mothers. Our findings, hence, provide insights for policymaking which targets labour market integration of migrant women.

title: Group threat and power-differential theories as differential predictors of religion-motivated hate crimes and the construction of local hate crime statistics
Racial/ethnic and educational disparities in married and cohabiting individuals’ propensity to form interracial unions
abstract: Prior research shows that cohabiting individuals are more likely than married individuals to form interracial unions. This pattern is frequently attributed to the perception of cohabitation as a lower-commitment union, which may lead single men and women to be less selective in choosing cohabiting partners than in choosing marital spouses. Yet, the meaning of cohabitation varies across groups: for some, it functions as a marriage-like union, while for others, it serves as a form of engagement, trial marriage, or an alternative to dating. This paper examines whether the gap in mate selection behavior by cohabitation status varies according to the role that cohabitation plays in the family life of different racial/ethnic, nativity, and educational groups. Using data from the 2008–2024 American Community Survey, we estimate log-linear models examining how the odds of forming interracial unions vary by cohabitation status as well as the partner's race/ethnicity, education, nativity status, and gender. Results confirm that cohabitation is more likely than marriage to involve partners of a different racial/ethnic background. The size of this gap varies by partner's race/ethnicity, nativity status, education, and gender. Specifically, among women, this gap is smallest among Hispanics and largest among Blacks. Among men, this gap is smallest among Hispanics and largest among Asian Americans. Overall, our findings reveal that mate selection behavior varies not only by union type (cohabitation or marriage) but also by partner's race/ethnicity, nativity status, education, and gender.

title: Separated in childhood: The long-term impacts of parental migration on educational attainment in China
abstract: This study investigates the long-term, gender-specific impacts of parental migration during childhood on educational attainment in adulthood. While migration can bring economic benefits through remittances, it also disrupts family caregiving arrangements, triggers emotional distress, and changes values and preferences. Using data from the China Family Panel Study, this article examines how paternal, maternal, and dual-parent outmigration before age 12 influences children's year of completed schooling by adulthood. The findings show that the father's outmigration is associated with an increase in educational attainment, particularly when the father leaves for shorter durations and in early childhood. Conversely, the mother's outmigration is associated with a reduction in years of education, with stronger impacts when the migration lasts longer (over 1 year) and occurs in later childhood (ages 4–12). The impact of parental outmigration also varies by the child's gender and rural-urban context.

title: Social origin, the class ceiling in earnings, and job task segregation: Evidence from Germany
abstract: Social class origin is closely linked to individuals' labor market outcomes. This study examines the class ceiling—the earnings disadvantage that those from lower-class origins experience within higher-class occupations. We propose that job task segregation, i.e., the non-random selection into different task profiles within granular occupations, contributes to the class ceiling. We study these dynamics in Germany, characterized by rigid social structures and low social mobility. Using high-quality survey data with individual measures of job tasks (National Educational Panel Study Adult Cohort), we estimate Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML) regression with a log link. Class origin effects on earnings are most pronounced in higher salariat positions, where individuals from privileged origins earn substantially more than their lower-origin counterparts, even within the same occupations. Job tasks differentials by social origin are visible; those from an advantaged background perform more analytical and creative job tasks, even within the same occupations. These differentials explain a small part of the earnings gap by class origin. The findings contribute to understanding the intergenerational transmission of advantage, particularly how class origin shapes outcomes within occupations.

title: Historical exception or historical continuity? Black-White disparities in long-term displacement from the City of New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina
abstract: Racialized population displacement is one of the mechanisms through which a disaster may entrench existing social structures and processes. The present study uses Hurricane Katrina's residential mobility and outmigration impacts on Black and White adults as a case study to explore this question. Drawing on a population-representative survey of pre-Katrina Orleans Parish (City of New Orleans) residents four to five years after Katrina, and on 1985-1990 and 1995-2000 decennial Census microdata, we first compared observed 2005-2009/10 mobility to mobility patterns of all Black and White Orleans Parish adults estimated in the absence of Katrina. Second, we used the survey data to counterfactually apply working-age White mobility rates to working-age Black Orleans Parish residents with equivalent housing damage and socio-economic characteristics, and vice versa. We estimated that 53,000, or almost one in four, Black Orleans Parish adult residents were displaced long term from the New Orleans metropolitan area, whereas at the population level White Orleans Parish residents suffered no displacement. Racial disparities in residential moves from Orleans Parish to suburban New Orleans parishes were crucial in explaining racial disparities in displacement from the metropolitan area. Had White working-age Orleans Parish residents suffered the same housing damage as Black residents and had equivalent socio-economic characteristics, 29% would have moved to suburban New Orleans parishes, versus an observed 4% of Black Orleans Parish residents who made such moves, indicating strong entrenchment of pre-Katrina residential racial stratification and segregation processes.

title: Editorial Board
Sibling group sex composition and gender-typical educational choices
abstract: Educational choices are heavily stratified by gender. In this study we examine whether an important structural factor in the family of origin, sex composition of the sibling group, affects the emergence of the gender-typed preferences that may drive these choices. Using Swedish population register data, we use multinomial logistic regression models to examine educational choices at upper-secondary school (N = 424,788) and university (N = 133,222) for first-born Swedish men and women in two-child sibling groups, with analyses based on cohorts born 1980–2003. We further examine whether there are any differences in educational choices by parental educational level. We focus on first-born children in two-child families, and we present supplementary analyses for second-born children. We find that men in two-child sibling groups with brothers are more likely to apply for female-dominated upper-secondary programs than men with sisters, while men with sisters are significantly more likely to follow some male-dominated tracks than men with brothers. These differences are concentrated amongst men raised by parents with lower education. However, we do not find that sex composition is associated with university subject choices for men, and we do not find any differences in educational choices for women by the sex composition of the sibling group. These results suggest some support for the predictions that a mixed sex sibling group can lead to a more gender-typed upbringing for men.

title: Vertical and horizontal educational stratification in risk of subjective status loss
The intersection of gender and education in care work: How work from home reshaped care-related travel
abstract: The COVID pandemic expanded work-from-home (WFH) access beyond highly educated groups, potentially reshaping gendered divisions of care. Drawing on doing gender, absolute resources and the time-flexibility framework, this study examines how WFH affects care-related travel in German cities, focusing on gender and educational inequalities. Care-related travel is a significant yet frequently disregarded component of unpaid labor, thus making mobility data crucial for capturing gender differences when WFH. Using representative mobility data from the Mobility in Germany (2017, n=14,421) and Mobility under the Influence of the Coronavirus Pandemic (2022/2023, n= 695) surveys, I examine changes in WFH likelihood and daily care-related travel before and after COVID. OLS regressions estimate differences in care-related trips, while logistic regressions assess WFH probabilities by education and gender. The findings reveal distinct educational patterns in gender disparities. Before COVID-19, non-university-educated men were more likely to WFH than women, but this gender gap disappeared after the pandemic. WFH is associated with higher care-related mobility among non-university-educated women before and after the pandemic, while this association is weaker or absent among university-educated women. These findings suggest that WFH may reconfigure gendered care responsibilities in ways that differ by educational attainment, with care-related travel burdens increasing most clearly among women without a university degree.

title: Marriage endures, fertility evolves: Family dynamics and life satisfaction in China
Doing gender, doing health: Disentangling the relationship between gender and health lifestyles
Double robust, flexible adjustment methods for causal inference: An overview and an evaluation
abstract: Double robust methods for flexible covariate adjustment in causal inference have proliferated in recent years. Despite their apparent advantages in overcoming model misspecification, these methods are rarely used by social scientists. It is also unclear whether these methods actually outperform more traditional methods in finite samples. This paper has two aims: It is a guide to some of the latest methods in double robust, flexible covariate adjustment using machine learning, and it tests them against more traditional statistical methods and flexible, non-double robust methods using simulated, cross-sectional data where the treatment effect is known. Double robust methods covered include Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW), Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE), and Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DML). Results suggest that these methods do outperform traditional methods in a wide range of simulations, but only when paired with flexible machine learning estimators. Notably, G-computation with the same flexible estimators obtains almost identical results, and standard regression methods have only slightly higher bias. In the scenarios considered in this paper, flexibility and robustness to heterogeneous treatment effects appear to be more important properties than double robustness.

title: Flexible work and housework division in dual-earner couples in the UK: The role of relative bargaining power
abstract: Although flexible work arrangements (FWAs) are widely viewed as tools for reconciling work and family life and promoting gender equality in dual-earner households, they may instead reinforce traditional gender roles in domestic labor. Existing research often attributes men's limited domestic response to flexibility to the male breadwinner model and focuses on the moderating role of individual characteristics, thereby overlooking relational power dynamics that shape domestic labor allocation. Therefore, a dyadic perspective that explicitly accounts for couples' relative bargaining power measured by differences in income and occupational class is essential for clarifying when FWAs reinforce inequality and when they facilitate redistribution. Drawing on nationally representative panel data from the UK (2010-2024) and applying two-way fixed-effects models, this study shows that wives' use of FWAs is consistently associated with their higher share of housework, while husbands' use of FWAs is associated with wives' lower share of housework only when husbands hold lower bargaining power than their partners. Further analyses reveal heterogeneity across types of FWAs: reduced hours and remote work produce stronger redistributive effects toward husbands than flexi-time. The findings refine time availability and doing gender theories by showing that flexibility is conditional rather than inherently equalizing, and they underscore the importance of relative resources in shaping domestic labor outcomes.

title: Gender gaps in leisure association participation among children of immigrants: Cultural legacies, parental socialization, and peer contexts
abstract: This study examines gender gaps in participation in leisure associations, such as sports, music, anddrama clubs, among children of immigrants—a critical yet understudied aspect of immigrantintegration. Using V-Dem data on gender traditionalism in origin countries and survey data from fourWestern European societies (N ≈ 18,000), the authors analyze how cultural legacies, parentalsocialization, and peer contexts shape gendered participation in leisure associations. Results showthat girls from more gender-traditional countries participate markedly less in leisure associations thanthose from gender-egalitarian backgrounds, underscoring persistent cultural legacy influences. At themicro-level, parental socialization of traditional gender values significantly shapes girls’ participationbut only partially mediates cultural legacy influences from origin countries. Additionally, peers alsoinfluence gendered behaviors, often amplifying or mitigating gender gaps in leisure associationparticipation, highlighting the dual cultural pressures of parental and peer environments. Thesefindings contribute to ongoing debates on immigrant integration while offering novel insights into theintersections of gender, culture, and civic engagement.

title: Marriage in a divided world: Spousal political dissimilarities and marital conflict in Hong Kong
abstract: Amid escalating global affective polarization, this study examines the ramifications of within-couple political dissimilarities for marital relationships using representative dyadic data from Hong Kong (N = 1003 married couples)—the first such examination in a non-democratic, rapidly polarizing context. Drawing on value incongruence theory and the affective polarization literature, the study proposes three sets of hypotheses regarding the roles of spousal political identity and value dissimilarities in the frequency, scope, and intensity of marital conflict, as well as the moderating role of affective polarization. Regression analyses show that political identity dissimilarity is a robust and independent predictor of more frequent marital conflicts over political matters and relationship issues. Notably, identity dissimilarity is associated with a higher likelihood of spousal psychological aggression even after controlling for value dissimilarities and conflict frequencies, indicating that identity-based antagonism is not reducible to simply more frequent and broader disagreement. Affective polarization strengthens the associations between political identity dissimilarity and conflicts over non-political domains. Consequently, politically misaligned couples experience both more frequent conflicts across multiple domains and more intense conflicts, manifested as psychological aggression. Value dissimilarities, by contrast, exhibit weaker and less consistent links to conflict frequency and intensity. These results demonstrate that identity-based antagonism—amplified by the moralization of political orientations—drives marital strain beyond substantive policy or value disagreements.

Gender, sexual orientation, and intimate partner violence: Timing and cumulative exposure among U.S. adults
Patterns of racial identification among children of intermarried Asian Indians: Evidence from longitudinally and intergenerationally linked Census data
Kinship structure in contemporary China: Analysis based on covariation in perceived trustworthiness across kinship roles
A global view on educational differences in career success: Organizational sponsorship, accumulated advantage, and the schooled society
abstract: Despite education's dominance in the globalized knowledge economy, the ways and reasons why education impacts subjective and objective career success remain the object of debate. We propose a three-level contextual model to explain the effect of education on job satisfaction and work meaningfulness (indicators of subjective career success) and personal income (as indicator of objective career success). First, within the organizational context , employers rely on beliefs about school meritocracy to recruit and promote individuals, translating into differential opportunities for advancement that mediate education-based differences in career success. Second, considering the temporal context , educational differences in career success will increase throughout people's careers through processes of accumulated advantage. Age should thus moderate the education effect on career success. Third, the education effect should vary across cultural contexts , depending on the extent to which a society has become ‘schooled’. We test these claims using multi-level, multi-source data from 33,120 employees across 44 countries, sourced from the International Social Survey Programme, in combination with archival country-level data. Results from multilevel mediation and regression analyses show that (1) organizational sponsorship statistically mediates the education effect on career success to a significant extent, (2) educational disparities in work meaningfulness and personal income widen at higher age, and (3) there is partial evidence for cross-cultural variation in how education shapes career success. Our findings show that the education effect on career success is highly context-dependent and suggest that schooling should be understood not only as a reflection of economic and technological factors but also as a (global) cultural force.

title: When satisfied workers lose faith: Perceived coworker dissatisfaction and organizational attachment
abstract: Personal job satisfaction is a key driver of organizational attachment, but to what extent do workers' perceptions of their coworkers' job satisfaction also matter? We measure perceived coworker dissatisfaction in a national quota sample of Canadian employees (n = 996) and argue that perceptions of discontent may function as a broader reading of the organization's health and trajectory that matters for attachment over and above workers' own job experiences. Prior to testing whether these perceptions matter, we document a substantial gap between perception and report. On average, study participants estimate that 41% of their coworkers are dissatisfied with their jobs, well above the 24% rate of personal dissatisfaction in the sample. Because workers are themselves coworkers, an accurate average estimate should match the actual rate of coworker dissatisfaction in the Canadian working population; the gap we observe instead indicates that perceptions are systematically inflated in the aggregate. While we cannot gauge the accuracy of these perceptions for any individual participant, multivariate analyses reveal that they are associated with lower organizational commitment and higher turnover intentions, particularly among satisfied workers. These findings suggest that satisfied workers—those for whom collective discontent is most discrepant from personal experience—are most attuned to cues about coworker discontent. Moreover, because such overestimation is common, this dynamic may operate even in workplaces where few workers are dissatisfied. We discuss implications for how organizations communicate employee sentiment back to their workforce.

title: Marriage boundaries: A network approach to occupational assortative mating in the United States
abstract: This study examines patterns in occupational assortative mating in the United States from 1970 to 2023 using a network-based cluster approach. Unlike previous research that relies on predefined occupational classifications, we inductively detect marriage boundaries to capture how detailed occupations group into marriage-relevant clusters. Drawing on data from the 1970–2000 U.S. Censuses and the 2001–2023 American Community Survey, we construct weighted occupational marriage networks, identify marriage classes through community detection, and track changes in boundary rigidity over time. Results reveal pronounced clustering: individuals disproportionately marry within distinct occupational clusters rather than across them. These inductively detected clusters diverge substantially from conventional class schemes, demonstrating that marriage markets operate according to a distinct social-distance logic. Crucially, we uncover a divergence between homogamy and boundary rigidity. While homogamy has risen steadily under fixed classifications, rigidity follows a different decline–rebound–stabilize trajectory: declining from the 1970s through the 1990s, rebounding in the 2000s, and stabilizing thereafter at levels generally below the 1970 baseline. This pattern is consistent with shifts in occupational structure and the emergence of bridge occupations that connect otherwise distinct clusters. These findings challenge the assumption that rising homogamy necessarily signals tightening social closure and show instead that the structure of marriage boundaries—the occupations that cluster together and the permeability of those clusters—has reorganized in ways not captured by fixed occupational schemes.

title: Upward educational mobility and life satisfaction: Mobility patterns, gender inequalities and age trajectories
abstract: Research on the implications of intergenerational educational mobility for subjective well-being has paid little attention to heterogeneity across mobility patterns and different groups. To address this gap, we examine how upward educational mobility affects life satisfaction, focusing on three aspects: First, we distinguish mobility patterns by the distance between educational origin and destination. Second, we assess the mediating role of income and occupational position. Third, we examine heterogeneities by age and gender. Using 39 waves of the German Socio-Economic Panel Study, we apply inverse probability weighting and a fixed effects approach to compare the life satisfaction of upwardly mobile individuals to counterfactual outcomes had they remained at their parental educational level. Our results show that upward educational mobility is related to increased life satisfaction and that this effect amplifies with age. Differences in life satisfaction between mobile and non-mobile individuals are partly driven by unequal labor market returns, but labor market processes do not explain the age-related increase in mobility effects. Despite persistent gender inequalities in social roles and rewards of educational attainment in the German context, the impact of mobility on life satisfaction is largely similar for women and men. Overall, the findings support the rising-from-rags hypothesis and cumulative advantage theory, indicating that upward educational mobility yields enduring improvements in life satisfaction.

title: The role of intergenerational social mobility in subjective social status: Comparing children of immigrants and children of natives
abstract: Subjective social status (SSS)—how individuals perceive their position within the social hierarchy—offers a unique lens for understanding the lived experience of social stratification. In immigrant families, where migration is often driven by aspirations for upward mobility, SSS may be particularly revealing of how the second generation evaluates its own socioeconomic integration. Yet, despite a growing literature on well-being and life satisfaction, the SSS of immigrants' descendants remains understudied, and little is known about how it is shaped by intergenerational social mobility. Drawing on the nationally representative French Trajectories and Origins 2 survey (2019–2020), this study uses diagonal reference models to examine how educational and occupational mobility influence the SSS of children of immigrants compared to children of natives. The findings reveal that the effects of intergenerational social mobility on individuals' SSS are not universal. Instead, their existence and strength vary markedly across gender and ethnic groups: downward mobility has a significant negative effect on the SSS of sons of natives, but not of sons of immigrants. By contrast, it strongly lowers the SSS of daughters of immigrants—particularly those of North African and Middle Eastern origin—while leaving that of natives’ daughters unaffected. We argue that these patterns reflect the interplay of parental expectations and deviation from traditional gender roles. These results position SSS as a crucial, yet overlooked, indicator for understanding the subjective dimension of immigrant incorporation and intergenerational mobility.

title: Neither settling nor conforming: expectations and reactions to low quality jobs of migrant-origin workers in the Netherlands
abstract: Migrant-origin workers in Western European countries are more likely to hold low-quality jobs compared to native-origin workers. According to adaptation-level and relative deprivation theories and theories of immigrant socioeconomic integration, this difference may result from migrant-origin workers having lower job quality expectations and weaker reactions to low-quality jobs, due to their awareness of structural labour market disadvantages and lower employability. However, these assumptions have rarely been tested empirically. We provide a direct test using longitudinal, high-quality survey data from the Netherlands (2008-2024) and comparing native-origin workers and first- and second-generation migrants (N = 3744-9671, across model specifications). We hypothesize that migrant-origin workers have lower job quality expectations, experience less job dissatisfaction when those expectations are unmet, and are less likely to translate job dissatisfaction into turnover intentions and subsequent job changes. Based on random- and fixed-effects regression models, we find that migrant-origin workers have similar wage and working hours expectations as native-origin workers. They also report similar or even higher levels of job dissatisfaction when their job quality expectations are unmet. When dissatisfied with their jobs, migrant-origin workers are as likely as native-origin workers to express turnover intentions. Despite their intentions being similar, migrant-origin workers are generally less likely to change jobs in the following year. Overall, our findings indicate that migrant-origin workers neither settle for nor conform to low-quality jobs, and that their structural disadvantage may be better explained by demand-side constraints.

title: The influence of refugees’ housing location on their social contacts: Evidence from a national quasi-experiment
abstract: In fleeing from war and persecution, refugees lose important social contacts from their home country and need to develop new social networks in their host country. A common conjecture is that the region where refugees settle has important influences on whether and with whom refugees develop social contacts, but establishing causal evidence has remained notoriously difficult. In this paper, we utilize the Dutch dispersal policy – which quasi-randomly allocates refugees across regions in the Netherlands – as a natural experiment to establish the causal effects of refugees' housing location on their social contacts. We use a representative longitudinal survey with 7387 observations from 3137 Syrian refugees in the Netherlands, merged with register data on the ethnic composition and urbanity of their housing region. We find that placing refugees in regions with a higher share of Dutch residents leads to more social contacts with the Dutch, and there is tentative evidence that it even leads to positive effects for social contacts within one's own origin group, and no effects on contacts with other migrants. Placing refugees in regions with a higher share of residents of Syrian descent leads to more social contacts only with other Syrians. These regional effects do not diminish over a period of five years. We find no robust effect of urbanity on social contacts. Altogether, our findings reveal how the ethnic composition of refugees' housing region shapes their social contacts, and suggest that dispersal policies can partly influence whether and with whom refugees develop social contacts.
